opening.text: How to install Nocturne, live with it on your desktop, and stay in charge of what it holds.

parts.text: You keep things as you go: a photo of a letter, a voice note, a file, a line of text. Nocturne reads them overnight while your computer is plugged in and idle (a catch-up after sleep may run on battery while it has 40 per cent or more), joins them up, and hands you one page each morning. Ask it a question and it answers only from what it can show you, with the originals it used underneath. Everything stays on this computer.
Nocturne is deliberately small. These are choices, not missing pieces you need to work around.

items.text: It does not print by itself. You can print the morning page whenever you choose to.
It does not remind you. It lists what needs you on the page and in the app, and sends one quiet note when the page is ready if you allow that. It never nags.
It speaks English (UK) only, for the app and for the spoken page.
It has no "Keep anyway". If you have already kept the same thing, Nocturne tells you when and keeps nothing new.
It does not open password-locked PDFs. Save an unlocked copy and drop that in instead.
It is not signed by Apple or Microsoft, so a Mac or Windows computer warns you the first time you open it. Install and remove shows what to click.

sections.heading: What this version does not do

opening.text: Nocturne meets your desktop in four places: a small icon in the tray, a quick keep shortcut, one notification and starting with your computer. Each has a plain fallback when your desktop does not offer it.

parts.text: When your desktop has a notification area, Nocturne puts a small icon there. It shows what Nocturne is doing (resting, reading, tidying, needs you, paused) and its menu lets you keep something, ask, open today's page, pause for an hour, until tonight or until you resume, and quit. Closing the window leaves Nocturne running in the tray, so the overnight tidy can still happen.
GNOME does not show a tray unless you add an extension that provides one (look for "AppIndicator" in your extensions app). Without a tray:

items.text: Closing the window quits Nocturne, and nothing is tidied while it is not running. Leave the window open or minimised overnight, or add the extension.
Nothing is lost either way. What you kept is safe, and Nocturne catches up on the next start.

parts.text: Most other desktops, such as KDE Plasma, show the tray without any extra step.

The default shortcut is Ctrl+Shift+Space on Windows and Linux, and Cmd+Shift+Space on a Mac. It opens a small box above whatever you are doing, where you can type, paste, drop a file or hold Space in the empty box to talk. Press Esc and it goes away. You can change the keys in

opening.text: Away from home lets your phone ask Nocturne a question, keep something and read today's page while you are out. It is off until you turn it on. Everything stays on your computer; your phone talks to it through a connection you choose, and what travels is sealed so that only your phone and your computer can read it.

items.text: if you have set it up before.
Choose a connection. Simple is the default and needs no account. Most private uses your own Tailscale account and is harder for anyone else to observe.
Nocturne asks before it downloads the small helper program the connection needs. Nothing is downloaded until you say yes.
Your computer must stay on and awake for the phone to reach it. Nocturne can keep it awake, but only while it is plugged in.

parts.text: Most private uses your own Tailscale account, and Nocturne walks you through what that account asks for. Each step opens the right Tailscale page in your browser, and Nocturne carries on by itself when you are done.

items.text: Sign in to Tailscale in your browser, in the page that opens.
If your Tailscale account asks for new computers to be approved, Nocturne says so and opens the page that lists this computer. Approve it there. It shows under a made-up name.
If your account does not allow secure links yet, Nocturne opens that page. Choose Enable HTTPS once.
Get Tailscale on your phone, if it is not there already.

parts.text: Tailscale can take a little while to make the secure address. Nocturne keeps trying. If it is still not ready after 30 seconds, Away from home shows a problem and keeps trying, then returns to normal when it works.

If your Tailscale account asks computers to keep a log of their activity for Tailscale, Most private refuses to join and says so in plain words, because it never sends logs. Use another account, or turn Away from home off.

If an iPhone is involved, add Nocturne to the home screen first and open it from there, so the phone keeps its key.

Ask a question, keep text, a photo, a document or a voice note, take back what it just kept, read today's page and the last seven, and open an original that an answer or the page cited. It never sees anything you marked private. It cannot forget, delete, export, change settings or add other phones.
If the phone has no signal, what it keeps waits on the phone and is sent when it connects again. That waiting list sits in the phone's own storage and is not hidden from someone who has the phone.
An unlocked or stolen phone can read everything not marked private until you remove it from the computer, so remove a lost phone first.
Content is sealed, so neither company can read your questions, your page or your files. They can see other things.

items.text: Your phone's internet address and rough place, a stable id for each phone, when it connects, and the size and timing of every message. Cloudflare also serves the code of the page your phone opens. The phone keeps that page so it opens without a connection, so a change Cloudflare makes, or someone who breaks into it, can stay on the phone until you add the phone again, and a changed page could misuse your phone's key while it is open. After your computer restarts, the phone looks for it at an old name that Cloudflare, or someone who later gets that name, answers. Nothing in the phone app can check this, so it is a known limit. A native phone app would later fix it. Most private makes it much harder: Tailscale would have to vouch for your computer's name in public, where anyone can see it. In Simple, anyone using your computer can also see the public address, though it does not let them in.

Your account, the computers on it and when they connect. When your phone and computer cannot connect directly, Tailscale carries the sealed traffic. Only your own devices on your Tailscale account can reach your computer. Other people's devices, tagged devices and devices shared with you are refused, and your own still need a code and your Allow to pair.

The helper also talks to its company's computers to stay connected while Away from home is on. Your computer may ask whether Nocturne's helper may accept connections. That is expected. It is why this feature is not described as staying on your own computer: while it is on, a helper uses your computer's network interfaces, not only its internal address.

What your provider sees is your question and those sentences, your internet address, and your key. It also sees one request for its list of services each time Nocturne's private engine starts while Online answers is on; that request holds none of your memories. Nocturne cannot check what your provider keeps or for how long, so read its own terms. Choose a service you already trust with that.

Online answers has no monthly limit unless you set one. You can limit the number of questions a month, or an amount in US dollars (only when your provider reports what each answer costs). When the limit is reached, answers come from this computer and Nocturne tells you once a month. The count starts again on the 1st. Nocturne shows money only if your provider reports the cost of an answer; otherwise it says the cost is "Not told". The site of your provider is where you see your real balance and set your own spending cap.

A backup is one file that holds everything Nocturne needs to start again on this or another computer. It is locked with a passphrase you choose, and nobody can open it without that passphrase. Export everything is for reading your things; a backup is for getting them back.

. Type a passphrase twice (at least 8 characters; Nocturne shows how strong it is), tick the box that says you have kept it safe, then choose where to save the file. Use a long one, such as three or four words that do not go together.
If you forget the passphrase, nobody can open the backup, not even the people who make Nocturne.
Keep it somewhere safe, apart from the file, or in a password manager. The file is named

Everything you kept, exactly as you kept it, everything Nocturne remembers from it, every page and your settings. Things you marked private are in it too, locked like the rest.

Nocturne has no account, no analytics and no crash reports. Its reading engine is a private one that listens only on your own computer's internal address, with a fresh key every time Nocturne starts.

Away from home and Online answers are the two exceptions, and each is off until you turn it on. While Online answers is on, your private engine sends a question and the few remembered sentences it needs to the one address you entered, and the Sent online log lists exactly what left (Online answers). While Away from home is on, sealed traffic goes to your own paired phones through the connection you chose, and that connection's helper talks to its company.
then shows what was sent to your phones, and Away from home lists what each company can see.
You do not have to take that on trust:

items.text: lists everything Nocturne ever downloaded, with the day and the size. Setup and any update you allowed are the only entries.
Nocturne only goes online to download what you agree to. It does not measure what a program sends while it runs, so it does not claim a figure for that.

Each release is checked to send nothing else. The people who build Nocturne run it with its network cut to the computer's own internal address, and treat every attempt to reach anywhere else as a failure. The check also confirms that Nocturne still starts, shows its window, runs its reading engine and keeps a file in that state. The result goes in the release notes.
You can run the same sort of check yourself: switch off your internet and use Nocturne. Nothing changes.

sections.heading: How you can tell nothing leaves your computer

opening.text: Choose a package for your computer, open it the first time, set Nocturne up, and take it off again.

items.text: It looks at your computer and tells you which setup it will use.

It downloads that setup once. It asks before it downloads. This is the only download Nocturne needs to start. You can keep things straight away while it downloads, and the download carries on by itself if the connection drops.
It tells you when it is ready. Your first page arrives the next morning.

parts.text: After setup, Nocturne works with no internet at all.
Removing the app does not remove what you kept. Your things stay in your data folder until you delete them yourself (see Your data).

items.text: Mac: drag Nocturne from Applications to the Bin.
Windows: open Settings, Apps, find Nocturne and choose Uninstall.
